entries.name: Angular artery right
entries.problem: Incorrectly makes the angular artery the usual source of the medial palpebral arteries.
entries.before: Angular artery: if present, this is the terminal branch of the [facial artery](#structure-artery.eca.facial.right). It may also originate from the ophthalmic or [infraorbital arteries](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.infraorbital.right). The vessel courses in the nasojugal fold giving off the medial palpebral artery supplying the eyelids, and anastomoses with the lateral palpebral artery ([lacrimal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.lacrimal_right)) to form the palpebral arcade. There are anastomoses with the ophthalmic, [lateral nasal](#structure-artery.eca.lateral_nasal.right), and [infraorbital arteries](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.infraorbital.right) in addition to its counterpart across the midline.
entries.after: The angular artery is a variable terminal continuation of the facial artery near the medial canthus. It supplies the adjacent nose and eyelids and communicates with dorsal nasal and other ophthalmic branches. Angular branches contribute to eyelid circulation, but the usual medial palpebral arteries arise from the ophthalmic circulation.

entries.name: Posterior deep temporal artery right
entries.problem: Ambiguous temporal-branch terminology; avoid an unsupported fixed origin.
entries.before: Posterior deep temporal artery: this arises at the level of the zygoma and is directed posteroinferiorly. Rarely it originates from the [IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.right) or from a common trunk with the zygomatico-orbital arteries. It supplies the temporalis muscle and anastomoses with the middle and anterior temporal arteries.
entries.after: This temporal muscular branch supplies the posterior temporalis and communicates with neighbouring temporal arteries. Deep temporal branches and branches of the superficial temporal artery form a variable anastomotic network.

entries.name: Mental artery right
entries.problem: Mostly describes the inferior alveolar bifurcation rather than this terminal branch.
entries.before: The [inferior alveolar artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.inferior_alveolar.right) divides into incisor and mental terminal branches opposite the first premolar tooth. The mental branch supplies the lower lip and chin.
entries.after: The mental artery is a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery. It leaves the mandible through the mental foramen and supplies the chin and lower lip, communicating with nearby facial and submental branches.

entries.name: Mylohyoid artery right
entries.problem: Generic extramandibular branches replace the named mylohyoid course.
entries.before: Extramandibular branches of the [inferior alveolar artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.inferior_alveolar.right) supply the pterygoid and mylohyoid muscles and the lingual nerve.

entries.name: Posterior superior alveolar artery right
entries.problem: Incorrect extension towards the incisive foramen; the named posterior alveolar territory was obscured.
entries.before:
Origin: this artery takes its origin from the proximal part of the third maxillary segment, just inside the pterygopalatine fossa. It often shares a common trunk with the [infraorbital artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.infraorbital.right).

Course: anteroinferiorly on the lateral surface of the maxilla, giving off osseous branches, supplying the mucosa of the maxillary sinus and buccal cavity, and buccinator. The vessel then enters the superior alveolar canal in the maxilla running towards the incisor foramen.

Anastomoses: [infraorbital](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.infraorbital.right), [transverse facial](#structure-artery.eca.superficial_temporal.transverse_facial.right), and [descending palatine](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.descending_palatine.right) arteries.
entries.after: The posterior superior alveolar artery usually arises from the maxillary artery near the pterygopalatine fossa. Branches enter posterior superior alveolar foramina and canals to supply the posterior maxillary teeth, adjacent gingiva and maxillary sinus. Its alveolar anastomoses include infraorbital arterial branches.

entries.name: Posterior septal artery right
entries.problem: Long discussion of a five-vessel anterior plexus replaces the posterior septal course.
entries.before: Posterior septal (or medial [sphenopalatine](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.sphenopalatine.right)) artery: this vessel is medially directed towards the superior turbinate and gives off a branch to the sphenoid ostium. It divides into superior and inferior branches. The superior branch supplies the superior turbinate before coursing medially to the nasal septum where it curves anteriorly. It anastomoses with branches of the [anterior ethmoidal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_ethmoidal_right) and [descending palatine](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.descending_palatine.right) and contributes to Kiesselbach’s plexus. This plexus is located on the anterior inferior quadrant of the nasal septum (‘Little’s area’) and is a common site for epistaxis. It is supplied by five vessels: the [sphenopalatine](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.sphenopalatine.right), [superior labial](#structure-artery.eca.superior_labial.right), greater palatine, [anterior ethmoidal](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_ethmoidal_right), and [posterior ethmoidal](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_ethmoidal_right) arteries.
entries.after: The posterior septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery reaches the nasal septum and runs anteriorly within its mucosa. It supplies the posterior septum and communicates with ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial territories.

entries.name: MMA frontal artery right
entries.problem: Orbital anastomoses dominate a description of the frontal meningeal division.
entries.before: Anterior convexity branches: these originate from the temporal, pterional, and coronal segments and course medially along the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. There are important anastomoses with the [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right). The [MMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.mma.right) may be the sole supply of the orbit (the ‘meningo-ophthalmic artery’) or supply the lacrimal gland and lateral orbit via a recurrent branch traversing the [foramen of Hyrtl](#structure-landmark.cranio-orbital.right) (found in the spheno-orbital foramen, in the orbital roof). This latter branch usually also has [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right) anastomoses. Anterior branches from the coronal segment anastomose with the [anterior ethmoidal](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_ethmoidal_right) branch of the [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right).
entries.after: The frontal division of the middle meningeal artery ascends over the sphenoidal and frontal convexity towards the coronal region, supplying the anterior supratentorial dura. It communicates with neighbouring meningeal territories and may give orbital or falcine connections.

entries.name: MMA orbital artery right
entries.problem: Conflates a local orbital branch with replacement of the entire ophthalmic supply.
entries.before: The [MMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.mma.right) may be the sole supply of the orbit (the meningo-ophthalmic artery) or supply the lacrimal gland and lateral orbit via a recurrent branch traversing the [foramen of Hyrtl](#structure-landmark.cranio-orbital.right). This latter branch usually also has [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right) anastomoses.
entries.after: An orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery can reach the lacrimal or orbital circulation through a cranio-orbital canal or connections near the superior orbital fissure. A meningolacrimal contribution and a meningo-ophthalmic origin are distinct patterns; neither is obligatory.

entries.name: Central retinal right
entries.problem: Incorrectly fixes the origin within the optic canal and fails to distinguish inner retinal supply.
entries.before: The central retinal artery: this, the most important branch, arises within the [optic canal](#structure-landmark.optic-canal.right) and travels alongside the optic nerve to supply the retina. It is a terminal branch without anastomoses and occlusion may result in permanent and severe visual loss.
entries.after: The central retinal artery usually arises from the ophthalmic artery within the posterior orbit, with variation in its origin and branching order. It pierces the optic nerve sheath and travels within the nerve to supply the inner retina. It behaves as a functional end artery; the outer retina is mainly supplied by the choroidal circulation.

entries.name: Posterior communicating right
entries.problem: Embryology is repeated and the actual named connection is not stated first.
entries.before:
The PCOM insertion defines the PCA P1-P2 segments. Embryonically, the PCOM represents the caudal division of the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) (contrasting with the adult description of the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) division into the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and anterior cerebral artery (ACA)).

A ‘fetal type’ PCOM, seen in approximately 25%, means the vessel is larger than the P1, or that it supplies most of the flow to the PCA territory. Complete absence of the PCOM is very rare; however, a very hypoplastic vessel may not be appreciated angiographically.

Branches: the PCOM gives off numerous small perforators to the ventral thalamus. These may be present even if the vessel is hypoplastic.

In embryonic development the PCOM is the caudal division of the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right). As the vertebrobasilar system develops and gives rise to the PCA, the PCOM regresses to a variable degree.
entries.after: The posterior communicating artery connects the supraclinoid internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery at the P1-P2 junction. Its calibre varies from hypoplastic to a dominant fetal configuration. Perforators contribute to the hypothalamic and anterior thalamic circulation.

entries.name: Inferior hypophyseal right
entries.problem: Embryological discussion of other clival vessels dominates this hypophyseal branch.
entries.before: The posterior inferior hypophyseal artery: anastomoses with its contralateral counterpart and supplies the posterior (and sometimes part of the anterior) lobe of the pituitary. It gives off an inferior clival artery that anastomoses with clival branches of the [hypoglossal artery](#structure-artery.eca.apa.hypoglossal.right). The posterior inferior hypophyseal and medial clival arteries are remnants of the primitive [IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.right) which can persist and enlarge in agenesis of the [cervical ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right.segment.cervical), so reconstituting the intracranial carotid circulation.
entries.after: The inferior hypophyseal artery, commonly a meningohypophyseal branch, supplies mainly the posterior pituitary and communicates with its opposite-side counterpart. Small associated branches may supply adjacent sellar and clival dura.

entries.name: ACA pericallosal right
entries.problem: Segment-by-segment parent narrative obscures the named distal arterial axis.
entries.before:
The A2 segment arises distal to the [ACOM](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_communicating) and extends to the junction of the rostrum and genu of the corpus callosum.

The A3 segment extends around the genu of the corpus callosum.

Segments inclusive of and distal to the A3 are generally called the pericallosal artery, although sometimes the A2 segment is also referred to as such. Small perforating branches supply the corpus callosum and the callosal arteries, and these traverse the corpus callosum to supply the septum, anterior pillars of the fornix, and anterior commissure. Distally, there are anastomoses with the [posterior pericallosal branch of the PCA](#structure-artery.posterior.pca_splenial_right) via perisplenial branches.

The A4 segment originates at the body of the corpus callosum and the A5 segment is the continuation of the vessel posterior to the coronal suture.
entries.after: The pericallosal artery is the distal continuation of the anterior cerebral artery along the corpus callosum. It curves around the genu and continues in the pericallosal cistern, giving callosal and medial hemispheric branches. The precise use of the term and the origins of its cortical branches vary.

entries.name: Callosomarginal right
entries.problem: Overly fixed A3 origin and branch count.
entries.before: The callosomarginal artery is the major branch of the A3 segment and runs parallel to the vessel inside the cingulate sulcus. It may be absent, with its branches arising directly from the [pericallosal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.aca_pericallosal_right). It gives off four arteries that supply the medial frontal lobe: the anterior, middle, and posterior internal frontal arteries, and the [paracentral artery](#structure-artery.anterior.paracentral_right).
entries.after: The callosomarginal artery is a variable major branch of the distal anterior cerebral artery. It runs posteriorly in or near the cingulate sulcus and supplies medial frontal and paracentral territories. It may be absent, and its origin is not restricted to one ACA segment.

entries.name: Anterior internal frontal right
entries.problem: Parent branch list replaces the selected cortical territory.
entries.before: The anterior internal frontal artery is one of four branches of the [callosomarginal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.callosomarginal_right) supplying the medial frontal lobe. The [callosomarginal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.callosomarginal_right) may be absent, with its branches arising directly from the [pericallosal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.aca_pericallosal_right).
entries.after: The anterior internal frontal artery supplies the anterior medial frontal cortex. It may arise from the callosomarginal or pericallosal arterial system, with variable overlap with frontopolar and other internal frontal branches.

entries.name: MCA superior division right
entries.problem: Identical division-wide description, dominated by the parent MCA bifurcation rather than this M2/M3 division.
entries.before:
The artery usually divides into two trunks, although a single trunk, trifurcation, or quadrifurcation are all possible. Superior and inferior divisions are usually referred to. It is slightly more common for the inferior division to be dominant, covering the temporal and parietal lobes while the superior division tends to supply the frontal lobe. With superior dominance, its territory may extend to the angular gyrus and temporo-occipital regions.

The branches angulate superiorly and course in the Sylvian fissure lateral to the insular cortex.
entries.after: The superior division of the middle cerebral artery courses over the insula as an M2 trunk, then passes through the operculum as M3 branches to reach the cortex. It predominantly supplies the lateral frontal and perirolandic territories. Its branching pattern and territorial extent vary.

entries.name: MCA orbitofrontal right
entries.problem: Generic M4 discussion replaces the orbitofrontal branch anatomy.
entries.before:
The orbitofrontal artery is one of the frontal branches of the MCA. The cortical branches are named after the regions they supply.

The M4 (cortical) segments commence at the opercular turn and run on the surface of the cerebral convexity. The M4 cortical branches supply the cerebral convexity. The MCA as a whole also supplies the insular and opercular cortex through earlier branches, associated with the M2 insular and M3 opercular portions.
entries.after: The MCA orbitofrontal artery supplies the lateral orbital surface of the frontal lobe. It may arise as an early MCA branch or from the superior division, with variable overlap with ACA orbitofrontal supply.

entries.name: Lateral lenticulostriate 1 right
entries.problem: Unresolved phrase "this segment" and mixed medial/lateral perforator territories.
entries.before: Lenticulostriate arteries (between 1 and 20, average 10) arise from the superior surface of this segment and perforate the anterior perforated substance. The medial group supplies the globus pallidus and lentiform nucleus. The lateral group supplies the anterior commissure, internal capsule, and upper head and body of the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, and substantia innominata. They have an S-shape configuration on the right, and reverse S-shape on the left. The medial group may also arise from the A1 and the latter group may arise from the M2 segments.
entries.after: A representative lateral lenticulostriate artery arises from the MCA, most often its M1 segment, and enters the anterior perforated substance. These perforators supply variable portions of the striatum, pallidum and internal capsule. The numbered branches are illustrative and do not imply a fixed number or identical territories.

Medial branches supply the anterior aspect of the lateral wall of the third ventricle, hypothalamus, and septum pellucidum. Inferior branches infiltrate the optic nerves and chiasm. They vary in size and number.
entries.after: The medial lenticulostriate arteries are small ACA perforators supplying the anterior basal ganglia and adjacent anterior internal capsule. Their number, origin and overlap with the recurrent artery of Heubner and other ACA perforators vary.

entries.name: Vertebral right

entries.before: The vertebral artery can be divided into four segments.
entries.after: The vertebral artery usually arises from the subclavian artery, ascends through the cervical transverse foramina and enters the cranial cavity near the foramen magnum. The paired intradural vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. Its conventional segments are V1 preforaminal, V2 foraminal, V3 atlantal and V4 intradural.

entries.name: Thalamoperforator 1 right
entries.problem: Broad list overstates a fixed shared territory for every numbered perforator.
entries.before: Posterior thalamoperforators (up to eight): these enter the posterior perforated substance, the interpeduncular cistern, and medial cerebral peduncles, and supply the posterior part of the thalamus, posterior part of the optic chiasm and tracts, posterior limb of the internal capsule, hypothalamus, subthalamus, substantia nigra, red nucleus, oculomotor and trochlear nuclei, rostral mesencephalon, and cerebral peduncles. The peduncular supply includes the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.
entries.after: A representative posterior thalamoperforating artery arises from the proximal posterior cerebral artery and enters the posterior perforated substance. This variable perforator group supplies the paramedian thalamus and parts of the rostral midbrain. The numbered examples do not represent fixed individual territories.

The anterior thalamoperforating group also supply the posterior optic chiasm, proximal optic radiations, posterior hypothalamus, and cerebral peduncle. They anastomose with choroidal arteries.
entries.after: A representative perforator from the posterior communicating artery contributes to the hypothalamic and anterior thalamic circulation. The tuberothalamic artery is a variable named member of this group; it is not synonymous with every PCom perforator.

entries.after: A medial hemispheric branch of the superior cerebellar artery supplies the medial part of the superior cerebellar hemisphere, with overlap with superior vermian branches. The SCA division pattern is variable.

entries.name: PICA medullary perforator right
entries.problem: Describes the first three parent segments rather than the selected medullary branch.
entries.before: The first three [PICA](#structure-artery.posterior.pica_right) segments emit perforators to the lateral medulla and anterior and lateral spinal arteries. The perforators may anastomose with those from the vertebral and [basilar artery](#structure-artery.posterior.basilar).
entries.after: A medullary perforator from the proximal PICA enters the medulla, commonly contributing to its lateral territory. Number, entry site and overlap with direct vertebral perforators vary.

entries.name: Posterior spinal right
entries.problem: Irrelevant comparison with MCA perforators and a fixed normal diameter distract from the spinal artery.
entries.before:
The PSAs are positioned off midline, and hence identifiable on carefully performed true AP spinal angiography. They are sometimes visible arising from the intradural vertebral arteries or [posterior inferior cerebellar arteries](#structure-artery.posterior.pica_right), particularly in the presence of cervical AVMs. In the non-pathological state, they are small and measure <0.5 mm.

The PSAs and contributing radiculopial arteries create a network to supply the circumference of the periphery of the cord in a centripetal manner. In this instance, the network is analogous to the M2 perforators as they pass into the insular cortex from the Sylvian fissure.

The PSAs principally supply the posterior third of the cord, including the dorsal columns, dorsal grey matter, and dorsal aspects of the lateral columns.
entries.after: The paired posterior spinal arteries descend on the dorsolateral spinal cord and usually arise cranially from the vertebral arteries or PICAs. Together with radiculopial and pial contributions, they supply the posterior cord, especially the dorsal columns and posterior grey matter.

entries.after: A representative paramedian pontine artery arises from the basilar artery and penetrates the ventral pons near the midline. These perforators supply medial pontine territories; the numbered examples do not specify fixed universal branches.

entries.name: Pontine circumferential right
entries.problem: Implies that long branches fully encircle the pons.
entries.before:
Short circumflex branches partially encircle the pons.

Long circumflex branches fully encircle it and generally have fewer terminal branches.
entries.after: Circumferential pontine branches curve around the lateral pons. Short branches supply ventrolateral regions, while longer branches reach more lateral or dorsal territories; their origins and contributions vary.

entries.name: Medial clival MHT branch right
entries.problem: Description starts with another vessel and is dominated by embryology.
entries.before: The [posterior inferior hypophyseal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.inferior_hypophyseal_right) gives off an inferior clival artery that anastomoses with clival branches of the [hypoglossal artery](#structure-artery.eca.apa.hypoglossal.right). The [posterior inferior hypophyseal](#structure-artery.anterior.inferior_hypophyseal_right) and medial clival arteries are remnants of the primitive [IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.right).
entries.after: The medial clival branch of the meningohypophyseal system supplies the medial clival dura. It communicates with clival branches of the ascending pharyngeal artery and with opposite-side clival channels.

entries.after: The inferior muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery supplies the inferior rectus, inferior oblique and other adjacent orbital muscles according to the branching pattern. It communicates with infraorbital and other orbital branches.

entries.name: Deep recurrent ophthalmic right
entries.problem: Copied ILT ramus description reverses the focus of the selected ophthalmic branch.
entries.before: The anteromedial ramus is directed towards the [superior orbital fissure](#structure-landmark.superior-orbital-fissure.right), supplying CNs III, IV, V1, and the abducens nerve (CN VI), and forming an anastomosis with the [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right) as the deep recurrent ophthalmic artery.
entries.after: The deep recurrent ophthalmic artery runs posteriorly from the ophthalmic circulation towards the superior orbital fissure and communicates with the anteromedial inferolateral trunk. It is an orbital-cavernous collateral route with a variable calibre and origin.

entries.name: Lacrimal inferior branch right

entries.after: A masseteric branch of the facial artery supplies the adjacent masseter and communicates with masseteric branches of the maxillary and transverse facial arteries.

entries.after: The superior medial palpebral artery usually arises from the ophthalmic circulation and supplies the medial upper eyelid. It joins lateral palpebral branches in the upper lid arcades; angular artery contributions are variable.

entries.after: A parotid branch of the transverse facial artery supplies the parotid gland and adjacent tissues. It is distinct from the continuing facial and masseteric branches.

entries.name: Zygomatico-orbital right
entries.problem: Incorrect muscle name "orbicularis orbis" and an unspecified parent bifurcation.
entries.before: Zygomatico-orbital artery: this arises just proximal to the bifurcation and is directed anteriorly along the upper border of the zygomatic arch towards the lateral angle of the orbit. The artery supplies the anterior temporal and malar region and orbicularis orbis.
entries.after: The zygomatico-orbital artery is a variable superficial temporal branch running anteriorly along the upper border of the zygomatic arch. It supplies the lateral orbital and malar region, including orbicularis oculi, and communicates with adjacent facial and orbital arteries.

entries.name: Superior tympanic right
entries.problem: Second paragraph switches to the anterior tympanic artery.
entries.before:
The superior tympanic artery is a [petrosal branch of the MMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.mma.petrosal.right) supplying the tensor tympani muscle and superior part of the tympanic cavity.

The [anterior tympanic artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.anterior_tympanic.right) anastomoses in the tympanic cavity with the [inferior tympanic](#structure-artery.eca.apa.inferior_tympanic.right), superior tympanic, and [caroticotympanic](#structure-artery.anterior.caroticotympanic_right) arteries.
entries.after: The superior tympanic artery commonly arises from the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. It supplies the tensor tympani region and upper tympanic cavity and communicates with other tympanic arteries.

entries.name: Superior tympanic left

entries.after: The superior tympanic artery commonly arises from the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. It supplies the tensor tympani region and upper tympanic cavity and communicates with other tympanic arteries.

entries.name: Artery of superior orbital fissure right
entries.problem: Incorrectly routes the orbital-apex vessel through the sphenopalatine foramen into the nose.
entries.before:
Origin: superomedially from the third maxillary segment. It may share a common trunk with the [artery of the foramen rotundum](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.foramen_rotundum.right).

Course: superiorly through the [sphenopalatine foramen](#structure-landmark.sphenopalatine-foramen.right) towards the [superior orbital fissure](#structure-landmark.superior-orbital-fissure.right).

Anastomoses: anteromedial branch of the [ILT](#structure-artery.anterior.inferolateral_trunk_right) and recurrent meningeal branch of the lacrimal branch of the [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right).
entries.after: The artery of the superior orbital fissure is a variable branch of the pterygopalatine maxillary artery. It ascends from the pterygopalatine fossa towards the orbital apex and superior orbital fissure, where it can communicate with the anteromedial inferolateral trunk and ophthalmic circulation.

entries.name: Superior pharyngeal tubal branch right
entries.problem: Long account of a separate carotid branch distracts from the tubal branch.
entries.before:
The [superior pharyngeal branch](#structure-artery.eca.superior_pharyngeal.right) gives off an Eustachian tube branch, which supplies the Eustachian tube and submucosa of the fossa of Rosenmüller.

The [superior pharyngeal branch](#structure-artery.eca.superior_pharyngeal.right) of the [pharyngeal trunk](#structure-artery.eca.apa.pharyngeal_trunk.right) contributes to the Eustachian tube anastomotic circle. It is connected to the [petrous ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right.segment.petrous)’s mandibular and vidian arteries and forms connections with the [accessory meningeal artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.accessory_meningeal.right) and [pterygovaginal artery](#structure-artery.eca.pterygovaginal.right) (distal [IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.right)). It also sends a branch through the [foramen lacerum](#structure-landmark.foramen-lacerum.right) to the cavernous sinus, joining the [recurrent artery of the foramen lacerum](#structure-artery.amendment.ilt_recurrent_lacerum_ramus.right) and the [ILT](#structure-artery.anterior.inferolateral_trunk_right) from the [cavernous ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right.segment.cavernous).
entries.after: The tubal branch of the superior pharyngeal artery supplies the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube and adjacent nasopharyngeal mucosa. It communicates with accessory meningeal, pterygovaginal, vidian and mandibular arterial contributions around the tube.

entries.name: Superior pharyngeal tubal branch left

It also sends a branch through the [foramen lacerum](#structure-landmark.foramen-lacerum.left) to the cavernous sinus, joining the [recurrent artery of the foramen lacerum](#structure-artery.amendment.ilt_recurrent_lacerum_ramus.left) and the [ILT](#structure-artery.anterior.inferolateral_trunk_left) from the [cavernous ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_left.segment.cavernous).

entries.name: Falx cerebelli artery right
entries.problem: Describes the broader hypoglossal branch system rather than the named dural vessel.
entries.before: Posterior branches of the [hypoglossal artery](#structure-artery.eca.apa.hypoglossal.right) course inferomedially along the floor of the posterior fossa, medially as the artery of the falx cerebelli and laterally as the posterior meningeal artery. Both of these may also arise from the vertebral or [posterior inferior cerebellar arteries](#structure-artery.posterior.pica_right).
entries.after: The artery of the falx cerebelli ascends within the small dural fold between the cerebellar hemispheres. It arises variably from posterior meningeal, ascending pharyngeal, vertebral or PICA-related dural branches.

entries.problem: Treats the red nucleus and subthalamus as structures within the cerebral peduncle.
entries.before: The cisternal branches of the [anterior choroidal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_choroidal_right) supply the cerebral peduncle, including the corticospinal tracts, red nucleus, and subthalamus.
entries.after: A peduncular branch of the anterior choroidal artery supplies part of the cerebral peduncle, including descending motor-fibre territories. Its distribution overlaps variably with other peduncular perforators.

entries.name: Terminal ICA perforator 1 right
entries.problem: Unresolved "this segment" and disease discussion replace the selected perforator anatomy.
entries.before: This segment contains a variable number of perforating arteries to the anterior perforating substance, which contribute to the collateral reconstitution in Moyamoya disease. Anastomoses are found with the posterior choroidal arteries and ACA.
entries.after: A representative perforator from the terminal internal carotid artery enters the anterior perforated substance and contributes to deep forebrain supply. The number and territories of these perforators vary. They may enlarge in collateral networks in occlusive disease.

entries.before: Short callosal perforating arteries: supplying the pillars of the fornix and the anterior commissure.
entries.after: Short callosal branches of the distal anterior cerebral artery supply adjacent portions of the corpus callosum. They form a variable perforating network along the pericallosal arterial axis.

entries.before: Long callosal arteries: supplying adjacent cortex.
entries.after: Long callosal branches run along or over the corpus callosum and contribute to adjacent callosal and medial hemispheric territories. Their course and relationship to other pericallosal branches vary.

entries.name: Polar temporal right
entries.problem: Generic cortical branch naming text omits the temporal pole.
entries.before: The polar temporal artery is one of the temporal cortical branches of the MCA. These branches are named after the regions they supply.
entries.after: The polar temporal artery supplies the temporal pole. It commonly arises as an early temporal branch of the MCA, with variable origin and overlap with the anterior temporal artery.

entries.name: VA medullary perforator 1 right
entries.problem: Conflates a variable group of vertebral perforators with a single pontomedullary entry route.
entries.before: Perforators supplying the medulla and pyramids traverse the foramen caecum on the anterior medulla at the pontomedullary junction and penetrates all the way back to the tegmentum and floor of the fourth ventricle.
entries.after: A representative direct medullary perforator arises from the intradural vertebral artery and enters the medulla. It contributes to medullary territories with variable overlap with anterior spinal and PICA perforators; there is no single obligatory entry through the foramen caecum.

entries.after: The common cochlear branch of the labyrinthine arterial system supplies the cochlea through its cochlear branches and may give vestibulocochlear contributions. Branching patterns vary; it is distinct from the anterior vestibular artery.

entries.after: The anterior vestibular artery arises from the labyrinthine arterial system and supplies the anterior vestibular apparatus, including utricular and semicircular canal territories. It is distinct from the cochlear branches.

entries.after: Short circumferential pontine arteries arise from the basilar system and curve around the ventrolateral pons to supply lateral pontine territories. Their number and distribution vary.

entries.problem: Incorrect "fully encircle" description.

entries.after: Long circumferential pontine branches reach the lateral and dorsal pons, with contributions from the basilar and cerebellar arterial systems. They do not form a complete ring around the pons.

entries.after: Short circumferential PCA branches curve around the cerebral peduncle and supply neighbouring peduncular and tegmental territories. Their origin may be from P1 or P2.

entries.name: ICA petrous right
entries.problem: Incorrect stellate-ganglion attribution and imprecise segment start.
entries.before:
From the [carotid canal](#structure-landmark.carotid-canal.right) to the petrolingual ligament (approximately the anterior aspect of the petrous ridge).

Course: the segment starts vertically in the [carotid canal](#structure-landmark.carotid-canal.right) before turning anteromedially and running over the cartilage covering the [foramen lacerum](#structure-landmark.foramen-lacerum.right). It is accompanied by sympathetic fibres from the stellate ganglion and a venous plexus.
entries.after: In the NYU classification, the petrous ICA extends from entry into the carotid canal to the petrolingual ligament. Its vertical and horizontal portions pass through the petrous temporal bone and over the cartilage of the foramen lacerum. It is accompanied by sympathetic fibres derived from the superior cervical ganglion and by a venous plexus.

entries.name: ICA paraophthalmic right
entries.problem: Replaces a mesh-estimated starting point with the stated NYU anatomical definition and removes an absolute imaging claim.
entries.before:
From the estimated distal border of the cavernous segment, just proximal to the [ophthalmic artery](#structure-artery.anterior.ophthalmic_right) ostium, to the ostium of the [PCOM](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_communicating_right).

This segment incorporates the proximal and distal dural rings (the clinoid [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) segment); however, the dural anatomy in the anterior clinoid region is complex, variable, and impossible to reliably define on imaging, making it difficult to differentiate intradural and extradural aneurysms in this region.

The NYU classification includes the clinoid and dural-ring transition within the paraophthalmic segment. The regional ring boundary is estimated here; the atlas does not resolve a separate dural-ring surface.
entries.after: In the NYU classification, the paraophthalmic ICA extends from the estimated proximal dural ring to the posterior communicating artery origin. It includes the clinoid and ophthalmic regions and therefore spans the transition from extradural to intradural ICA. The ophthalmic origin alone does not reliably identify the distal dural ring.

entries.name: ACA A2 right

The A3 segment extends around the genu of the corpus callosum.

entries.after: The A3 segment of the ACA curves around the genu of the corpus callosum in the pericallosal cistern. It continues into the supracallosal distal ACA; callosomarginal and cortical branch origins vary.

entries.name: Anterior choroidal right
entries.problem: Very broad territory list and an incorrect parenthetical placement of the red nucleus and subthalamus within the cerebral peduncle.
entries.before:
The anterior choroidal artery supplies highly eloquent tissue. It is rarely absent. It usually arises posterolaterally from the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right), 2-4 mm distal to the origin of the [PCOM](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_communicating_right). It may uncommonly arise from the MCA, a joint origin with the [PCOM](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_communicating_right), or the [PCOM](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_communicating_right) itself. It may also be larger than the [PCOM](#structure-artery.anterior.posterior_communicating_right), and thus occasionally mistaken for this vessel.

The anterior choroidal artery runs posteriorly beneath the optic tract and then around the cerebral peduncle in the carotid, crural, and ambient cisterns before again crossing the optic tract from medial to lateral at the level of the lateral geniculate body. It then enters the choroidal fissure and terminates in the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle. Occasionally, it may sweep around the pulvinar to reach the foramen of Monro. It anastomoses with the posterior choroidal artery via its intraventricular terminal branches and also with the middle and posterior cerebral arteries.

The crucial branches are cisternal. They supply the optic tract, cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tracts, red nucleus, subthalamus), the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic radiation, the lateral geniculate body, proximal optic radiations, the hippocampus, the amygdala, the uncus, dentate gyrus, piriform cortex, globus pallidus, and the ventral thalamic nuclei. Although a small artery, its occlusion may cause significant neurological deficit, including contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral hemisensory loss, contralateral homonymous hemianopia, hemineglect, and aphasia.
entries.after: The anterior choroidal artery usually arises from the supraclinoid ICA distal to the posterior communicating artery. It follows the optic tract and medial temporal region before entering the choroidal fissure to supply the lateral ventricular choroid plexus. Cisternal branches contribute variably to the optic tract, posterior internal capsule, pallidal, peduncular and medial temporal territories; these are not identical in every individual.

entries.name: Medial posterior choroidal right
entries.problem: Incorrect description of the velum interpositum as a small membrane; excessive subsidiary territory detail.
entries.before: Medial posterior choroidal artery: this vessel usually arises from the medial P2 segment but may arise from the parieto-occipital, calcarine, or posterior pericallosal (splenial) branches. It runs medially and supplies the adjacent tectum, pineal gland, habenula and medial geniculate body, and posterior thalamus. It then enters the roof of the third ventricle within the velum interpositum (the small membrane just above and anterior to the pineal gland) to supply the choroid plexus. As it arches over the quadrigeminal plate, it adopts a characteristic ‘3’ shape on a lateral angiographic projection. It runs inferior to the [lateral posterior choroidal arteries](#structure-artery.posterior.lateral_posterior_choroidal_right). Terminal branches anastomose with the [lateral posterior choroidal arteries](#structure-artery.posterior.lateral_posterior_choroidal_right) at the foramen of Monro.
entries.after: The medial posterior choroidal artery usually arises from the proximal PCA, often P2, and curves around the midbrain towards the roof of the third ventricle. It enters the velum interpositum region to supply choroid plexus and gives variable branches to adjacent pineal, tectal and thalamic territories.

entries.name: Posterior meningeal VA right

entries.before: Posterior meningeal artery: the posterior meningeal artery supplies the tentorium cerebelli and may originate from the extracranial [vertebral artery](#structure-artery.posterior.vertebral_right), the [occipital artery](#structure-artery.eca.occipital.right), the [ascending pharyngeal artery](#structure-artery.eca.apa.right), or the [PICA](#structure-artery.posterior.pica_right).
entries.after: A posterior meningeal branch of the vertebral artery contributes to posterior cranial fossa dura, often approaching the foramen magnum region. It communicates with occipital, ascending pharyngeal and other meningeal branches; posterior meningeal arterial origins vary.

entries.name: ICA cervical right
entries.problem: Detailed nerve-position assertions distract from the segment and include an unnecessary accessory-nerve claim.
entries.before:
This begins at the bifurcation of the [CCA](#structure-artery.anterior.common_carotid_right) and ends as the artery enters the [carotid canal](#structure-landmark.carotid-canal.right).

Course: the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) is contained within the carotid sheath, anteromedial to the IJV. The [ECA](#structure-artery.carotid.external.right) is also usually anteromedial initially, before it veers laterally. The vagus nerve and the cranial root of the accessory nerve are located posteriorly.
entries.after: The cervical ICA extends from the common carotid bifurcation to the external opening of the carotid canal. It ascends in the carotid space with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve and normally gives no branches in the neck.

entries.name: Lateral lenticulostriate 2 right
entries.problem: Unresolved phrase "this segment" and mixed medial/lateral perforator territories.
entries.before: Lenticulostriate arteries (between 1 and 20, average 10) arise from the superior surface of this segment and perforate the anterior perforated substance. The medial group supplies the globus pallidus and lentiform nucleus. The lateral group supplies the anterior commissure, internal capsule, and upper head and body of the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, and substantia innominata. They have an S-shape configuration on the right, and reverse S-shape on the left. The medial group may also arise from the A1 and the latter group may arise from the M2 segments.
entries.after: A representative lateral lenticulostriate artery arises from the MCA, most often its M1 segment, and enters the anterior perforated substance. These perforators supply variable portions of the striatum, pallidum and internal capsule. The numbered branches are illustrative and do not imply a fixed number or identical territories.

The M4 (cortical) segments commence at the opercular turn and run on the surface of the cerebral convexity. The M4 cortical branches supply the cerebral convexity. entries.before: A large mastoid branch often continues superiorly and then enters the cranium through the [mastoid foramen](#structure-landmark.mastoid-foramen.right) to supply the posterior fossa dura mater: the posterior meningeal artery. It divides into descending, ascending, and posteromedial branches. The descending branch courses along the sigmoid sinus and anastomoses with the sigmoid sinus branch of the [ascending pharyngeal](#structure-artery.eca.apa.right). The ascending branch runs posterosuperiorly along the sigmoid sinus before anastomosing with the [petrosquamous branch of the MMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.mma.petrosquamosal.right) and sometimes the [subarcuate branch](#structure-artery.amendment.aica_subarcuate.right) of the [AICA](#structure-artery.posterior.aica_right). The posteromedial branch courses inferomedially and anastomoses with the hypoglossal, jugular, and musculospinal branches of the [ascending pharyngeal](#structure-artery.eca.apa.right), or the jugular branch of the [posterior meningeal artery from the vertebral artery](#structure-artery.posterior.posterior_meningeal_va_right).

entries.before: Paramedian arteries: these are the terminal branches of the [MMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.mma.right). They are directed anteriorly or posteriorly along the superior sagittal sinus and anastomose with the anterior (from the [anterior ethmoidal artery](#structure-artery.anterior.anterior_ethmoidal_right)) or posterior (from the [ascending pharyngeal](#structure-artery.eca.apa.right)) falcine arteries. entries.name: Frontal cortical vein right

entries.before: Cortical veins drain regions of the cerebral cortex into nearby sinuses. The peripheral medial surfaces drain to the [superior sagittal sinus](#structure-vein.superior_sagittal). Bridging veins cross the subdural space and may fuse with meningeal veins before entering a major sinus.
entries.after: Frontal cortical veins drain the frontal surface through a variable superficial venous network. Superior and medial channels commonly reach the superior sagittal sinus, while inferior frontal channels may join superficial Sylvian or basal drainage.

entries.name: External jugular vein right
entries.problem: Incorrectly includes the superficial temporal vein as a separate obligatory contributor at the EJV origin.
entries.before: The EJV drains the deep face, scalp, and posterolateral neck. It originates from the convergence of the retromandibular, posterior auricular, and superficial temporal veins in front of the angle of the mandible. The vein runs caudally on top of the sternocleidomastoid to join the subclavian vein. Like the IJV, it has a valve just prior to its termination.
entries.after: The external jugular vein usually forms from the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein. It descends superficially across sternocleidomastoid and usually drains into the subclavian vein. Its formation and tributaries vary.

entries.name: Pterygoid venous plexus right
entries.problem: Restricts a three-dimensional plexus to a single interval between temporalis and lateral pterygoid.
entries.before: The pterygoid plexus is a large venous network located between the temporalis and lateral pterygoid muscles. It drains into the [maxillary vein](#structure-vein.maxillary.right) and connects with the [cavernous sinus](#structure-vein.cavernous.right) via emissary veins. The plexus receives numerous tributaries, including the sphenopalatine, middle meningeal, deep temporal, pterygoid, masseteric, buccinator, alveolar, and palatine veins. It also receives blood from the [inferior ophthalmic vein](#structure-vein.inferior_ophthalmic.right), [deep facial vein](#structure-vein.deep_facial.right), and infraorbital vein.
entries.after: The pterygoid venous plexus occupies the infratemporal region around the pterygoid muscles, with superficial and deep components. It drains predominantly through the maxillary vein and communicates with the facial vein, orbital veins and cavernous sinus through variable channels.

entries.name: Facial vein right
entries.problem: Generic assertion that veins mirror arteries obscures the facial vein's own course and drainage.
entries.before: The extracranial drainage of the head and neck mirrors the arteries. The supratrochlear and supraorbital veins drain to the facial vein, which is a tributary of the [internal jugular vein](#structure-vein.internal_jugular.right). The [deep facial vein](#structure-vein.deep_facial.right) connects with the pterygoid plexus.
entries.after: The facial vein begins near the medial canthus as the continuation of angular venous drainage and descends across the face. It commonly joins the anterior retromandibular division to form the common facial vein draining to the internal jugular vein. It communicates with the ophthalmic veins and pterygoid plexus; venous patterns vary.

entries.after: The superior ophthalmic vein begins in the anterior superomedial orbit and runs posteriorly towards the superior orbital fissure to drain into the cavernous sinus. entries.name: Emissary vein of foramen ovale right
entries.problem: Generic emissary-vein paragraph does not centre the selected foramen and endpoints.
entries.before: Emissary veins are inconstant channels and serve as two-way connections linking extracranial veins, diploic veins, and intracranial meningeal veins and sinuses. Emissary veins passing through the skull foramina include those of the foramen ovale. The [pterygoid plexus](#structure-vein.pterygoid_plexus.right) connects with the [cavernous sinus](#structure-vein.cavernous.right) via emissary veins.
entries.after: The emissary vein of the foramen ovale is a variable communication between the cavernous sinus region and the pterygoid venous plexus through the foramen ovale. Its calibre and haemodynamic direction vary.

entries.name: Posterior communicating vein
entries.problem: Calling this variable venous channel constant is too absolute.
entries.before: The posterior communicating vein is a constant vessel in the interpeduncular fossa. This, in addition to hypothalamic and ventral mesencephalic veins, contributes to the posterior aspect of the venous circle.
entries.after: The posterior communicating vein is a transverse venous communication in the interpeduncular region linking the basal venous systems. Together with adjacent hypothalamic and mesencephalic channels, it may contribute to a posterior venous circle; its development and calibre vary.

entries.name: Superior sagittal sinus
entries.problem: Overly fixed claim that Trolard is always the largest superficial tributary.
entries.before: The superior sagittal sinus extends from the foramen caecum to the [confluence of sinuses](#structure-vein.confluence). It is located within the superior attachment of the falx to the calvarium. It receives the superficial cerebral veins from the medial and lateral cerebral hemispheres, the largest of which is the vein of Trolard.
entries.after: The superior sagittal sinus runs in the attached superior margin of the falx cerebri towards the confluence of sinuses. It receives superficial cerebral bridging veins and meningeal and diploic tributaries. The vein of Trolard may provide a major lateral hemispheric connection, but individual venous dominance varies.

entries.name: Vein of Galen
entries.problem: Clarify the selected deep collector and avoid an overly fixed termination landmark.
entries.before: This short subarachnoid vessel is formed by the midline convergence of the internal cerebral veins, below the splenium, beneath which it curves. It ends at the tentorial hiatus apex, where it joins the [inferior sagittal sinus](#structure-vein.inferior_sagittal) to become the [straight sinus](#structure-vein.straight). The vessel also receives blood from the posterior pericallosal veins, the internal occipital veins, and veins of the posterior fossa.
entries.after: The great cerebral vein of Galen is a short deep venous trunk beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum. It receives the internal cerebral veins and variable basal and posterior fossa tributaries, then joins the inferior sagittal venous system at the anterior end of the straight sinus.

entries.name: Inferior petrosal sinus right
entries.problem: Assigns the entire venous pathway to a fixed jugular pars nervosa corridor.
entries.before: These sinuses run inferiorly and laterally to connect the posterior aspect of the [cavernous sinus](#structure-vein.cavernous.right) to the [jugular vein](#structure-vein.internal_jugular.right) in the pars nervosa. They also receive blood from the internal auditory veins and infratentorial structures.
entries.after: The inferior petrosal sinus runs along the petro-occipital junction from the cavernous sinus towards the jugular bulb or upper internal jugular vein. Its jugular termination and connections with clival and infratentorial veins vary.

entries.after: The inferior petrosal sinus runs along the petro-occipital junction from the cavernous sinus towards the jugular bulb or upper internal jugular vein. Its jugular termination and connections with clival and infratentorial veins vary.

entries.name: Basal vein of Rosenthal right
entries.problem: Fixed formation and termination wording underrepresents recognised basal venous variation.
entries.before: The basal vein of Rosenthal originates under the anterior perforated substance in the chiasmatic cistern medial to the uncus of the temporal lobe, runs posteriorly, and terminates in either the [vein of Galen](#structure-vein.galen) or [internal cerebral vein](#structure-vein.internal_cerebral.right). It is formed by the confluence of the [anterior cerebral vein](#structure-vein.anterior_cerebral.right) and [deep middle cerebral vein](#structure-vein.deep_middle_cerebral.right). Its second segment encircles the cerebral peduncle, and its third segment is located behind the midbrain. It connects to the superior petrosal sinus via the [lateral mesencephalic vein](#structure-vein.lateral_mesencephalic.right).
entries.after: The basal vein of Rosenthal is a deep venous collector beginning near the anterior perforated substance, commonly receiving anterior cerebral, deep middle cerebral and inferior striate drainage. It courses around the midbrain and usually reaches the Galenic system. Its segments may be incomplete and alternative petrosal, tentorial or other drainage routes occur.

entries.name: Superior petrosal vein right
entries.problem: Absolute largest-vein claim and a broad list of unrelated venous groups.
entries.before: The superior petrosal vein, or petrosal vein, is the largest vein in the posterior cranial fossa. It drains the anterior cerebellum and brainstem into the [superior petrosal sinus](#structure-vein.superior_petrosal.right). It is usually formed by multiple smaller veins converging into one, but sometimes there are two or three. Major contributors include the vein of the cerebellopontine fissure, and the petrosal, posterior mesencephalic, anterior pontomesencephalic, and tentorial groups.
entries.after: The superior petrosal vein is a major collector of the petrosal cerebellar surface and adjacent brainstem. One or several trunks enter the superior petrosal sinus, receiving variable cerebellopontine fissure, peduncular and pontine tributaries.

entries.name: Foramen lacerum right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before:
The [petrosal ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right.segment.petrous) runs over the cartilage covering the foramen lacerum.

The [vidian artery from the IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.pterygoid_canal.right) runs through the [vidian canal](#structure-landmark.pterygoid-canal.right) to the foramen lacerum, where it meets the [vidian branch of the petrous ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.vidian_ica_contribution_right).
entries.after: The foramen lacerum lies at the junction of the sphenoid, petrous temporal and basilar occipital regions and is largely filled by cartilage in life. The internal carotid artery passes over its superior aspect rather than through an open vertical lumen. Petrosal neural and small vascular connections relate to this region.

entries.name: Tympanic canaliculus left
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [inferior tympanic artery](#structure-artery.eca.apa.inferior_tympanic.right.left) is directed superiorly through the canal of Jacobson ([inferior tympanic](#structure-artery.eca.apa.inferior_tympanic.right.left) canaliculus) to enter the tympanic cavity.
entries.after: The tympanic canaliculus opens near the jugular fossa and carotid canal and ascends to the middle ear. It carries the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve and the inferior tympanic artery.

entries.name: Jugular foramen and fossa right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [jugular branch](#structure-artery.eca.apa.jugular.right) of the [neuromeningeal trunk](#structure-artery.eca.apa.neuromeningeal_trunk.right) enters the cranium through the jugular foramen. It supplies the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves in addition to meninges.
entries.after: The jugular foramen lies between the temporal and occipital bones and transmits cranial nerves IX, X and XI with the sigmoid-jugular and inferior petrosal venous drainage pathways. The jugular fossa accommodates the jugular bulb.

It supplies the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves in addition to meninges.
entries.after: The jugular foramen lies between the temporal and occipital bones and transmits cranial nerves IX, X and XI with the sigmoid-jugular and inferior petrosal venous drainage pathways. The jugular fossa accommodates the jugular bulb.

entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [hypoglossal branch](#structure-artery.eca.apa.hypoglossal.right) of the [neuromeningeal trunk](#structure-artery.eca.apa.neuromeningeal_trunk.right) enters the cranium through the hypoglossal canal to supply the hypoglossal nerve and meninges.
entries.after: The hypoglossal canal traverses the occipital bone above the occipital condyle. It transmits the hypoglossal nerve, a venous plexus and small meningeal arterial branches.

entries.name: Mastoid foramen right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: A large mastoid branch of the [occipital artery](#structure-artery.eca.occipital.right) often enters the cranium through the mastoid foramen to supply the posterior fossa dura mater as the posterior meningeal artery.
entries.after: The mastoid foramen is a variable opening in or near the occipitomastoid region. It transmits the mastoid emissary vein and often a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.

entries.name: Foramen magnum
entries.problem: Incorrectly equates vertebral passage through the atlanto-occipital membrane with intradural entry.
entries.before: The V4 segment of the vertebral artery pierces the atlanto-occipital membrane to become intradural, entering the cranial cavity via the foramen magnum.
entries.after: The foramen magnum is the large occipital opening between the posterior cranial fossa and vertebral canal. It transmits the medulla-spinal cord transition, meninges, vertebral and spinal vessels and ascending spinal accessory roots. Vertebral dural entry is distinct from passage through the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane.

entries.name: Sphenopalatine foramen right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [sphenopalatine artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.sphenopalatine.right) passes medially through the sphenopalatine foramen to enter the nasal cavity, which it supplies in addition to the paranasal sinuses.
entries.after: The sphenopalatine foramen connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the nasal cavity at the superior palatine-sphenoid region. It transmits sphenopalatine vessels and associated nasal neural branches.

entries.name: Pterygoid (Vidian) canal right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The vidian artery, running horizontally, arises from the distal [IMA](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.right) and runs through the vidian canal to the [foramen lacerum](#structure-landmark.foramen-lacerum.right), where it meets the [vidian branch of the mandibulovidian artery](#structure-artery.anterior.vidian_ica_contribution_right) from the [petrous ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right.segment.petrous).
entries.after: The pterygoid or vidian canal runs through the base of the pterygoid process between the foramen lacerum region and pterygopalatine fossa. It contains the nerve and vessels of the pterygoid canal.

entries.name: Palatovaginal / pharyngeal canal right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The pharyngeal ([pterygovaginal](#structure-artery.eca.pterygovaginal.right)) artery courses posteromedially and inferiorly through the pharyngeal canal to supply the roof of the pharynx and pharyngeal end of the Eustachian tube.
entries.after: The palatovaginal or pharyngeal canal communicates between the pterygopalatine fossa and roof of the nasopharynx. It carries the pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery and an accompanying pharyngeal nerve.

entries.name: Greater palatine canal right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [descending palatine artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.descending_palatine.right) enters the greater palatine canal accompanied by the great palatine nerve. Within the canal it gives off the [lesser palatine artery](#structure-artery.eca.lesser_palatine.right), which supplies the soft palate.
entries.after: The greater palatine canal descends from the pterygopalatine fossa towards the palate, between the maxillary and palatine regions. It carries the descending palatine vessels and palatine nerves.

entries.after: The greater palatine canal descends from the pterygopalatine fossa towards the palate, between the maxillary and palatine regions. It carries the descending palatine vessels and palatine nerves.

entries.name: Greater palatine foramen right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [descending palatine artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.descending_palatine.right) becomes the [greater palatine artery](#structure-artery.eca.greater_palatine.right) as it exits the canal through the greater palatine foramen. It courses anteriorly beneath the hard palate to supply the hard palate, gingiva, and nasal septum.
entries.after: The greater palatine foramen opens on the posterolateral hard palate. It transmits the greater palatine neurovascular bundle, which then runs anteriorly along the palate.

entries.name: Mandibular canal right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [inferior alveolar artery](#structure-artery.eca.maxillary.inferior_alveolar.right) enters the mandibular canal through an opening on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus and then courses anteroinferiorly and medially towards the [mental foramen](#structure-landmark.mental-foramen.right) on the anterior surface of the mandible.
entries.after: The mandibular canal runs within the mandible from the mandibular foramen on the medial ramus towards the mental and incisive pathways. It contains the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels.

entries.name: Atlas vertebral artery groove right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The [vertebral artery](#structure-artery.posterior.vertebral_right) imprints a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas, which may rarely form a bony ring called the [arcuate foramen](#structure-landmark.arcuate-foramen.right) (a possible risk factor for paediatric ischaemic stroke).
entries.after: The vertebral artery groove lies on the superior surface of the posterior arch of the atlas. The extradural vertebral artery crosses it before turning towards its dural entry.

entries.after: An arcuate foramen is a variable bony bridge over the vertebral artery groove of the atlas. When present, it partly or completely roofs the regional vertebral neurovascular corridor.

entries.name: Petrolingual boundary (estimated) right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before:
From the [carotid canal](#structure-landmark.carotid-canal.right) to the petrolingual ligament (approximately the anterior aspect of the petrous ridge).

From the petrolingual ligament to the proximal dural ring.
entries.after: The petrolingual ligament forms a regional boundary between the petrous and cavernous ICA in the NYU classification. It extends near the petrous apex and sphenoid lingula; its position is estimated in this atlas.

entries.name: Anterior clinoid process right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: The anterior clinoid process is superolateral to the genu of the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right). Dural coverage extends medially to the tuberculum sellae from the anterior clinoid process. The dural ring is denser and more tightly adherent superolaterally and slopes inferomedially across the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) so the medial and posterior aspects of the [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) genu can lie in the subarachnoid space.
entries.after: The anterior clinoid process is the medial projection of the lesser sphenoid wing beside the optic canal and clinoid ICA. It relates to the optic strut, proximal and distal dural rings and the carotid-oculomotor region.

entries.name: Proximal and distal dural ring region right
entries.problem: Description centres on an artery passing through the landmark instead of the opening, connections and contents.
entries.before: This segment incorporates the proximal and distal dural rings (the clinoid [ICA](#structure-artery.anterior.internal_carotid_right) segment); however, the dural anatomy in the anterior clinoid region is complex, variable, and impossible to reliably define on imaging, making it difficult to differentiate intradural and extradural aneurysms in this region.
entries.after: The proximal and distal dural rings bound the short clinoid ICA region. The distal ring marks the usual transition to the intradural ICA, with a variable carotid cave medially. This atlas marks a regional estimate rather than separately segmented dural rings.
